concepts.title: Linearity of the Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform and its inverse are linear transformations, meaning they preserve the weighted sum of signals.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform and its inverse are linear transformations:
$$\alpha \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] + \beta \ell_2 \left[ n,m \right]  
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\alpha \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] + \beta \mathscr{L}_2 \left[ u,v \right]$$
where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complex numbers. This property can be easily proven from the definition of the DFT. @fig-colorDFT shows a color visualization of the complex-value matrix for the 1D DFT.
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity allows us to analyze complex signals by breaking them down into simpler components, processing them individually, and summing the results.
concepts.recap_md: - The DFT of a linear combination of signals is the same linear combination of their individual DFTs.

concepts.title: Separability of the Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: If an image can be written as a product of two 1D signals, its Fourier transform is also the product of two 1D Fourier transforms.
concepts.content: An image is separable if it can be written as the product of two 1D signals, $\ell\left[n,m \right] = \ell_1\left[n \right] \ell_2\left[m \right]$. If an image is separable, then its Fourier transform is separable: $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u \right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[v \right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Separability simplifies the computation of the 2D DFT by allowing it to be performed as a sequence of 1D transforms, significantly reducing computational complexity.
concepts.recap_md: - A separable image $\ell[n,m] = \ell_1[n]\ell_2[m]$ has a separable Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}[u,v] = \mathscr{L}_1[u]\mathscr{L}_2[v]$.

concepts.title: Parseval's Theorem
concepts.one_liner: Parseval's theorem states that the dot product and norm of signals are preserved (up to a constant factor) after a Fourier basis change.
concepts.content:
As the DFT is a change of basis, the dot product between two signals and the norm of a vector is preserved (up to a constant factor) after the basis change. This is stated by Parseval's theorem:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] \ell_2^* \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] \mathscr{L}_2^* \left[u,v \right]$$
In particular, if $\ell_1=\ell_2$ this reduces to the Plancherel theorem:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \ell\left[n,m \right] \|^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \|^2$$
This relationship is important because it tells us that the energy of a signal can be computed as the sum of the squared magnitude of the values of its Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem ensures that the total energy of a signal is conserved when moving from the spatial domain to the frequency domain, which is vital for signal analysis and compression.
concepts.recap_md: - The dot product of two signals is proportional to the dot product of their Fourier transforms.

concepts.title: Convolution Property of the Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The operation of circular convolution in the spatial domain is equivalent to point-wise multiplication in the Fourier domain.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution is computationally expensive in the spatial domain; converting it to multiplication in the frequency domain allows for much faster filtering and image processing.
concepts.recap_md: - Circular convolution in space corresponds to multiplication in the frequency domain.

key_passage.text: Thus, the operation of a convolution, in the Fourier domain, is just a multiplication of the Fourier transform of each term in the Fourier domain: $$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \left[n,m\right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$

concepts.title: Dual Convolution Property
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the product of two images is the circular convolution of their individual discrete Fourier transforms.
concepts.content:
When working with images, we often perform products, such as applying a mask (multiplying the image by a mask with zeros in specific pixels). The Fourier transform of the product of two images is the (circular) convolution of their DFTs:

$$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \ell_2 \left[n,m\right]
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\frac{1}{NM} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \circ \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains how spatial masking or windowing affects the frequency spectrum of an image, which is critical for understanding artifacts in spectral analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Multiplication in the spatial domain corresponds to circular convolution in the frequency domain, scaled by $1/NM$.

concepts.title: Shift Property (Translation in Space)
concepts.one_liner: Translating a signal in the spatial domain results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential.
concepts.content:
A shift corresponds to a translation in space. Translating a signal in the spatial domain results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential. For an image $\ell[n,m]$ with Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$, displacing the image by $(n_0, m_0)$ pixels yields:
$$\mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n-n_0,m-m_0 \right] \right\} = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}$$
In practice, this property strictly holds for circular shifts due to the periodic assumptions of the DFT. For non-circular translations (like camera motion), it serves as an approximation because new pixels appear at boundaries. 

(see figure: Translation in space. Image (c) corresponds to image (a) after a translation of 16 pixels to the right and four pixels down. Images (b) and (d) show the real parts of their corresponding DFTs (with...)

Estimating the displacement between images can be done by locating the maximum in the inverse DFT of the ratio between their DFTs, though this method is not always robust in practice.
concepts.motivation_md: The shift property allows for the estimation of motion or alignment between images by looking at phase changes in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - A spatial shift results in a phase shift in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Modulation Property (Translation in Frequency)
concepts.one_liner: Multiplying an image by a complex exponential or wave translates its Fourier transform in the frequency domain.
concepts.content:
If we multiply an image with a complex exponential, its Fourier transform is translated:
$$\ell\left[n,m \right]  \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}}\mathscr{L}\left[u-u_0,v-v_0 \right]$$
A related relationship involving a cosine wave is:
$$\ell\left[n,m \right]  \cos{ \left( 2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\mathscr{L}\left[u-u_0,v-v_0 \right] + \mathscr{L}\left[u+u_0,v+v_0 \right]$$
Multiplying a signal by a wave is called signal modulation. This property is important in image analysis and communications. 

(see figure: Modulation in space. Multiplying an image by a cosine wave results in a new image with a Fourier transform with two copies of the Fourier transform of the original image. Only the magnitude of the...)

Note that shift and modulation are equivalent operations in different domains: a shift in space is a modulation in frequency, and a shift in frequency is a modulation in space.
concepts.motivation_md: Modulation is used to shift the frequency content of a signal, which is fundamental for tasks like encoding information or centering specific frequency components.

concepts.title: Matrix Form of the DFT
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform can be expressed as a linear transform using a symmetric matrix where each basis vector forms a row.
concepts.content:
As the DFT is a linear transform, we can write it in matrix form with one basis per row. In 1D, the matrix $\mathbf{F}$ for the DFT is as follows:

$$\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & \dots & 1\\ 
1 & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{1}{N} \right)} & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{2}{N} \right)} & \dots & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{N-1}{N} \right)}\\ 
1 & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{2}{N} \right)} & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{4}{N} \right)} & \dots & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{2\, (N-1)}{N} \right)}\\ 
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & ~ & \vdots \\
1 & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{(N-1)}{N} \right)} & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{(N-1)\, 2}{N} \right)} & \dots & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{(N-1)\, (N-1)}{N} \right)}\
\end{bmatrix}$$

Each entry in the matrix is $\mathbf{F}_{u,n} = \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)}$, where $u$ indexes rows and $n$ indexes columns. The matrix $\mathbf{F}$ is symmetric. The inverse of the DFT is the complex conjugate: $\mathbf{F}^{-1} = \mathbf{F}^{*}$. Working in 1D allows us to visualize the transformation matrix. Many Fourier transform properties and symmetries can be observed from inspecting this matrix, which yields the Fourier transform of 1D vectors when used as a multiplicand.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing the DFT as a matrix allows us to treat the transform as a standard linear algebraic operation. This formulation is useful for visualizing the transform's structure and for implementing it using optimized matrix-vector multiplication libraries.

concepts.title: Visualizing the Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The complex results of a DFT can be visualized using either real and imaginary components or polar amplitude and phase decompositions.
concepts.content:
When computing the DFT of a real image, we often use properties to interpret the result. As the DFT results in a complex representation, there are two possible ways of writing the result. 

Using the real and imaginary components:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = Re \left\{\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}  + j \, Imag \left\{\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}$$
where $Re$ and $Imag$ denote the real and imaginary part of each Fourier coefficient. 

Alternatively, using a polar decomposition:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j \, \theta\left[u,v \right]  \right)}$$
where $A \left[u,v \right] \in \mathbb{R}^+$ is the amplitude and $\theta \left[u,v \right] \in \left[-\pi, \pi \right]$ is the phase. 

(see figure: DFT of an image and visualization of (top) the real and imaginary components, and (bottom) the amplitude and phase of the Fourier transform.)
concepts.motivation_md: Because the Fourier transform produces complex numbers, it is difficult to visualize directly. Decomposing the result into amplitude and phase (polar) or real and imaginary parts makes the frequency information interpretable for humans.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of the Delta Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a discrete delta function is a constant value of 1 across all frequencies.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is:
$$\mathcal{F} \left\{ \delta \left[n,m \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \delta \left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = 1$$
This indicates the relationship $\delta \left[n,m \right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 1$. In terms of the inverse Fourier transform, this means that summing all complex exponentials with a coefficient of 1 results in a delta function at the origin, as all other values cancel out:
$$\delta \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=-N/2}^{N/2} \sum_{v=-M/2}^{M/2} \exp{ \left(2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$$

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of cosine and sine waves results in pairs of delta functions in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Symmetry and Separability of 2D Fourier Transforms
concepts.one_liner: Real and even input signals transform to real and even outputs, and separable 2D signals have DFTs that are products of 1D DFTs.
concepts.content: Real and even input signals transform to real and even outputs. For such signals, the magnitude of the Fourier transform is simply the absolute value of the real component, as the imaginary component is zero. Furthermore, if a 2D signal is separable (meaning it can be written as the product of two 1D signals), its DFT is also the product of the corresponding 1D DFTs.
concepts.motivation_md: Symmetry and separability are powerful properties that simplify the calculation and interpretation of 2D transforms. Separability, in particular, allows a 2D DFT to be computed as a series of 1D DFTs, which is much more efficient.

concepts.title: 2D Box Function
concepts.one_liner: A 2D box function is a separable function whose DFT is the product of two 1D box DFTs.
concepts.content:
A 2D box is a separable function and can be written as the product of two 1D box functions: $\text{box}_{L_n, L_m} \left[n,m\right] = \text{box}_{L_n} \left[n\right] \text{box}_{L_m}\left[m\right]$. Consequently, the DFT of a 2D box is the product of the two 1D DFTs:
$$\text{Box}_{L_n, L_m} \left[ u,v \right] = \text{Box}_{L_n} \left[ u\right] \text{Box}_{L_m} \left[ v\right].$$
concepts.motivation_md: The 2D box function is a standard model for rectangular apertures or simple image regions. Knowing its transform helps in understanding the frequency characteristics of rectangular filters and windowing effects in 2D.

concepts.title: The Box Function and its Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The box function is a rectangular signal whose Discrete Fourier Transform is a discrete sinc function.
concepts.content:
The box function is defined as follows:
$$\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] = 
\begin{cases}
    1       & \quad \text{if } -L \leq n \leq L  \\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise.} 
  \end{cases}$$
The box function takes values of 1 inside the interval $\left[ -L,L \right]$ and is 0 outside; its duration is $2L+1$. It can be viewed as a finite length signal of length $N$ with a periodic extension. 

[FIGURE:e9ca46281c35c8d1 | Box function for $L=5$ and $N=32$.]

To compute the DFT, we use the definition and the geometric series sum formula:
$$\mathcal{F} \left\{ \text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=-L}^{L} \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} = \frac{\sin \left( \pi u(2L+1)/N \right)}{\sin \left( \pi u/N \right)}$$
This result is known as the **discrete sinc** function. In summary, the DFT of the box function is:
$$\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right]\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{\sin \pi u (2L+1)/N}{\sin \pi u/N}$$
We denote this DFT as $\text{Box}_{L} \left[u \right]$. It is a symmetric real function with its maximum value at $u=0$.

(see figure: DFT of the box filter with $L=5$, and $N=32$.)
concepts.motivation_md: The box function is the simplest possible filter (an unweighted average). Understanding its Fourier transform is crucial because it reveals the 'ringing' artifacts (sidelobes) that occur when a signal is abruptly truncated in either the spatial or frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The box function has a value of 1 for $n \in [-L, L]$ and 0 elsewhere.

concepts.title: Discrete Sinc Function
concepts.one_liner: The discrete sinc function is a symmetrical periodic function that represents the DFT of a box function.
concepts.content:
The discrete sinc function **sincd** is defined as follows:
$$\text{sincd}(x;a) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{a \sin (\pi x/a)}$$
where $a$ is a constant. This is a symmetrical periodic function with a maximum value of 1.

concepts.title: A Family of Fourier Transforms
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform has a multitude of forms depending on the conventions used and the type of signal being analyzed.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform has a multitude of forms and it depends on the conventions used. When reading papers or other books that make use of the Fourier transform, you must carefully check how they are defining the transform before using it in your own analysis. The important thing is to be consistent in the formulation.

The Fourier transform also changes depending on the type of signal being analyzed. Although finite length discrete signals and images are common in practice, it is worth defining the Fourier transform for other signals such as continuous signals (functions of a continuous independent variable such as time) or infinite length discrete signals for which the standard Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) definition is not convenient.
concepts.motivation_md: Different mathematical and physical contexts require different versions of the Fourier transform. Understanding that a family of transforms exists ensures consistency when moving between continuous theory and discrete applications.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Fourier transform's specific form depends on the conventions of the author and the nature of the signal.
 - Consistency in the chosen formulation is critical for valid analysis.
 - Variants exist for continuous signals and infinite length discrete signals.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Continuous Signals
concepts.one_liner: The continuous Fourier transform is defined for infinite length signals using integrals to map time-domain functions to continuous frequency functions.
concepts.content:
The continuous domain is convenient when working with functions and operations that are not defined in the discrete domain. For instance, the derivative operator is well defined in the continuous domain but can only be approximated in the discrete domain. Similarly, the Gaussian distribution is defined as a continuous function. For these reasons, some formulations are easier when performed in the continuous domain.

For infinite length signals defined on the continuous domain, the Fourier transform is defined as:

$$\mathscr{L}(w) =  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell(t) \exp{ \left( - j w t \right)} \, dt $$

where $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a continuous function on the frequency $w$ (in radians). The inverse Fourier transform is as follows:

$$\ell(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{ \left( j w t \right) } \, dw$$

Most properties of the DFT apply to the continuous domain by replacing sums with integrals. The convolution between two continuous signals is defined as:

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) =  \ell_1 \circ \ell_2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_1 (t-t') \ell_2(t') \, d t'$$

These definitions can be extended to 2D by using double integrals across the spatial variables $x$ and $y$. While images and filters are discrete in practice, it is often convenient to treat them as continuous signals.
concepts.motivation_md: The continuous domain allows for exact mathematical operations, like differentiation, that are only approximated in discrete space. It provides a theoretical foundation for signals like the Gaussian distribution.
concepts.recap_md:
- The continuous Fourier transform uses integrals to transform infinite length signals into the frequency domain.
 - The inverse transform recovers the continuous signal from its frequency representation.
 - Convolution in the continuous domain is defined by an integral rather than a sum.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Infinite Length Discrete Signals
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform for infinite length discrete signals results in a continuous, periodic frequency representation.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform for discrete signals with infinite length is a useful tool where the sum becomes infinite. By replacing $w = 2 \pi u / N$, we can write:

$$\mathscr{L}(w) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell\left[n \right] \exp{(- j w n)}$$

The frequency $w$ is now a continuous variable. The Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a periodic function with period $2 \pi$.

The inverse Fourier transform is:

$$\ell\left[n \right] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{2 \pi} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{(j w n)} d w$$

where the integral is performed over exactly one period.
concepts.motivation_md: When signals are discrete but not limited to a finite window, the standard DFT is insufficient. This transform bridges discrete-time data with a continuous frequency spectrum.
concepts.recap_md:
- For infinite discrete signals, the Fourier transform involves an infinite sum and results in a continuous frequency variable.
 - The resulting frequency representation $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is periodic with a period of $2\pi$.
 - The inverse transform is calculated by integrating over one period of the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Summary of Fourier Transform Variants
concepts.one_liner: Fourier transforms vary based on whether the time and frequency domains are discrete or continuous, and finite or infinite.
concepts.content:
There are many variants of the Fourier transform. The three primary transforms used in this context are summarized below, all of which can be extended to 2D:

| Time Domain | FT | FT$^{-1}$ | Frequency Domain |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discrete time, Finite length ($N$) | $\mathscr{L} \left[u \right] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \ell \left[n \right] e^{-2 \pi j \frac{un}{N}}$ | $\ell \left[n \right] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \mathscr{L} \left[u \right] e^{2 \pi j \frac{un}{N} }$ | Discrete frequency, Finite length ($N$) |
| Continuous time, Infinite length | $\mathscr{L} (w) = \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \ell (t) e^{- j w t} dt$ | $\ell (t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L} (w) e^{j w t} d w$ | Continuous frequency, Infinite length |
| Discrete time, Infinite length | $\mathscr{L} (w) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell \left[n \right] e^{- j w n}$ | $\ell \left[n \right] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{2 \pi} \mathscr{L} (w) e^{j w n} d w$ | Continuous frequency, Finite length ($2 \pi$) |
concepts.motivation_md: Providing a summary of Fourier variants helps clarify which mathematical tool is appropriate for a given signal type (e.g., a digital image vs. a continuous wave).
concepts.recap_md:
- Finite discrete signals result in discrete, finite frequency spectra.
 - Continuous infinite signals result in continuous, infinite frequency spectra.
 - Infinite discrete signals result in continuous, periodic frequency spectra.

concepts.title: Amplitude and Phase Representation of the Fourier Transform

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of an image can be decomposed into amplitude and phase, representing intensity scaling and spatial location respectively.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform has been extensively used as an image representation. The Fourier transform of an image can be written in polar form:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j\, \theta\left[u,v \right]  \right)}$$
where $A \left[u,v \right] = \left| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \right|$ is the amplitude and $\theta \left[u,v \right] = \angle  \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is the phase.

Decomposing the Fourier transform into amplitude and phase is a useful representation. In terms of the inverse Fourier transform, $A \left[u,v \right]$ gives the strength of the weight for each complex exponential, while the phase $\theta \left[u,v \right]$ translates the complex exponential. The phase carries information about where image contours are by specifying how the phases of the sinusoids must line up to create observed edges. Translating an image in space only modifies the phase of its Fourier transform. In short, location information goes into the phase while intensity scaling goes into the magnitude.
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing a signal into amplitude and phase helps separate the 'what' (intensity/contrast) from the 'where' (structure/edges) in an image.
concepts.recap_md:
- Amplitude $A[u,v]$ represents the strength or intensity scaling of frequency components.
 - Phase $\theta[u,v]$ determines the spatial location and alignment of sinusoids to form contours.
 - Spatial translation of an image affects only the phase of its Fourier transform.

concepts.title: Relative Importance of Phase and Amplitude

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: In many natural images, the phase of the Fourier transform dominates the visual appearance and structural content over the amplitude.
concepts.content:
One might ask which is more important in determining the appearance of an image: the magnitude of the Fourier transform or its phase. (see figure: Swapping the amplitude and the phase of the Fourier Transform of two images. Each color channel is processed in the same way.)

A classical experiment involves computing the Fourier transform for two images and building new images by swapping their phases. The first output image uses the amplitude of the first input image and the phase of the second. The second output image uses the remaining terms. The results show that the appearance of the resulting images is mostly dominated by the phase. For example, an image built with the phase of a stop sign still looks like a stop sign, even if the amplitude comes from a different image. The phase signal determines where edges and colors are located, while changing the amplitudes primarily alters the final colors.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that phase carries structural information explains why preserving phase is critical in image processing tasks like reconstruction and compression.
concepts.recap_md:
- Swapping phases between two images shows that the resulting image visually resembles the source of the phase.
 - Phase determines the location of edges and structural features.
 - Amplitude influences the intensity and color balance but less of the recognizable structure.

concepts.title: Spectral Magnitude Decay in Natural Images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The magnitude of the Fourier transform for natural images typically peaks at the origin and decays inversely proportional to radial frequency.
concepts.content:
A remarkable property of natural images is that the magnitude of their DFT generally has its maximum at the origin and decays inversely proportional to the radial frequency. This magnitude is quite similar across different natural images and can be approximated by:
$$A \left[u,v \right] = a/ (u^2+v^2)^b$$
where $a$ and $b$ are constants. This typical structure of the DFT magnitude in natural images is often used as a prior for various tasks, such as image denoising.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that natural images share a common spectral power distribution allows engineers to create effective priors for image restoration and denoising.
concepts.recap_md:
- Natural images exhibit a spectral magnitude that decays as frequency increases.
 - The magnitude can be modeled by the power law $A[u,v] = a / (u^2+v^2)^b$.
 - This property serves as a statistical prior in image processing applications.

concepts.title: Experiment on Phase and Amplitude Information

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: While phase often dominates image structure, the relative importance of amplitude increases for periodic textures.
concepts.content:
(see figure: The relative importance of phase and amplitude depends on the image. Each row shows one image, its Fourier transform (amplitude and phase), and the resulting images obtained by applying the inverse Fourier transform to a signal with the original amplitude and randomized phase, and a signal with the original phase and a generic fixed $1/f$ amplitude. Note that for the first image, the phase seems to be the most important component. However, as we move down, the relative importance between the two components changes. And for the bottom image (showing a pseudo-periodic threat texture) the amplitude is the most important component.)

It is a misconception that all image information is contained solely in the phase. The amplitude also contains very useful information. To demonstrate this, consider an experiment where we compute the Fourier transform of an image and create two new versions: one keeping the original amplitude but randomizing the phase, and another keeping the original phase but replacing the amplitude with a noninformative generic form $A \left[u,v \right] = 1/(u^2+v^2)^{1/2}$. 

This generic amplitude is used because it produces a smoother image that reveals structure better than purely random noise. As shown in (Figure 1.1.6), the relative importance of these components changes depending on the image type. While phase carries most information for many scenes, for pseudo-periodic textures (like a thread texture), the amplitude becomes the most important component for defining the image content.
concepts.motivation_md: This experiment clarifies that the 'phase-is-everything' rule has exceptions, particularly for textures where periodic patterns are captured in the amplitude.
concepts.recap_md:
- Phase is generally more important for structural information in typical scenes.
 - Amplitude carries significant information for periodic or highly textured images.
 - Using a $1/f$ generic amplitude helps isolate the contribution of phase without introducing excessive noise.

concepts.title: Transfer function
concepts.one_liner: The transfer function is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel, representing how a filter reweights spectral components.
concepts.content: A convolution can be written as a product in the Fourier domain: [FIGURE:eb36ec0cfa3e5a10 | Transfer function of a linear filter.] The function $H \left[u, v \right]$ is called the **transfer function** of the filter. The transfer function of a filter is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel. The transfer function allows us to interpret filters by how they modify the spectral content of the input signal. As the Fourier transform of the output is just a product between the Fourier transform of the input and the transfer function, a linear filter simply reweights the spectral content of the signal. It does not create new content; it can only enhance or decrease the spectral components already present in the input.
concepts.motivation_md: The transfer function simplifies the analysis of filters by showing exactly how they enhance or decrease specific frequency components of a signal.

concepts.title: Amplitude gain
concepts.one_liner: Amplitude gain is the magnitude of the transfer function, representing the factor by which spectral components are scaled.
concepts.content: If we use the polar form: $$H \left[u,v \right] = \left|H \left[u, v \right] \right| \exp \left( {j \, \angle H \left[u, v \right]} \right) $$ The magnitude $\left| H \left[u, v \right] \right|$ is the **amplitude gain**. The magnitude at the origin, $\left| H \left[0, 0 \right] \right|$, is the **DC gain** of the filter (the average value of the output signal is equal to the average value of the input times the DC gain).
concepts.motivation_md: Amplitude gain quantifies how much a filter amplifies or attenuates specific frequencies, which is essential for designing filters like low-pass or high-pass systems.

concepts.title: Filter classification by frequency
concepts.one_liner: Filters are often classified by the frequency ranges they allow to pass, such as low-pass, band-pass, or high-pass.
concepts.content: The Fourier domain shows that, in many cases, what a filter does is to block or let pass certain frequencies. Filters are many times classified according to the frequencies that they let pass through the filter (low, medium, or high frequencies) as shown in (see figure: Sketch of the frequency responses of low-pass, band-pass, and high-pass filters.). When filtering images, low-pass filters will output a blurry picture encoding the **coarse** elements of the image. A band-pass filter will highlight middle size elements, while the output of a high-pass filter will show the **fine** details of the image. The three images in    show the output image processed by three filters corresponding to the frequency responses of low-pass, band-pass, and high-pass filters. There are many other properties of a filter that can be used to classify linear systems (e.g., causality, stability, phase-changes). Some filters have their main effect over the phase of the signal and they are better understood in the spatial domain. In general, filters affect both the magnitude and the phase of the input signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Classifying filters by frequency allows engineers to select the right tool for specific tasks, such as smoothing noise (low-pass) or detecting edges (high-pass).

concepts.title: Orthogonality of Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: Complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images, allowing any finite signal to be decomposed into a linear combination of these waves.
concepts.content: A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$, $$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$ Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a linear combination of complex exponentials.
concepts.motivation_md: Orthogonality ensures that each frequency component in a signal can be analyzed independently, which is the mathematical foundation for the Fourier Transform.
concepts.recap_md: - Complex exponentials serve as an orthogonal basis for finite discrete signals.- The inner product of two distinct basis elements is zero, while the inner product with itself is $MN$.- This property allows for the unique decomposition of any discrete image into frequency components.

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms a finite-sized image into a complex frequency-domain representation using a sum of complex exponentials.
concepts.content: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms an image $\ell\left[n,m \right]$, of finite size $N \times M$, into the complex image Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ as: $$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n,m \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)}$$ We will call $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ the Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: The DFT allows us to analyze the frequency content of digital signals and images, enabling tasks like filtering, compression, and feature extraction that are difficult in the spatial domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The DFT maps a spatial signal $\ell[n,m]$ to its frequency representation $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$.- It is computed by summing the product of the image and complex exponential basis functions.

concepts.title: Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform reconstructs a spatial signal or image from its complex frequency-domain representation.
concepts.content: By applying $\frac{1}{MN} \sum_{u=0}^{M-1} \sum_{v=0}^{N-1}$ to both sides of the Fourier transform equation and exploiting the orthogonality between distinct Fourier basis elements, we find the inverse Fourier transform relation: $$\ell\left[n,m \right] = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\} = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \exp{ \left(+2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$$
concepts.motivation_md: The inverse transform is essential for returning to the spatial domain after performing operations like noise reduction or sharpening in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The IDFT reconstructs the original signal $\ell[n,m]$ from its Fourier coefficients $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$.- It uses a positive exponent in the complex exponential and includes a normalization factor of $1/NM$.

concepts.title: Periodicity of the DFT
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform and its inverse are inherently periodic functions with periods corresponding to the dimensions of the input signal.
concepts.content: As $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is obtained as a sum of complex exponentials with a common period of $N,M$ samples, the function $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is also periodic: $\mathscr{L}\left[u+aN,v+bM \right] = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. Also, the result of the inverse DFT is a periodic image. Indeed, you can verify from the inverse Fourier transform equation that $\ell\left[n+aN,m+bM \right] = \ell\left[n,m \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding periodicity is crucial for correctly interpreting DFT results and avoiding artifacts like aliasing or edge effects when processing finite-length signals.
concepts.recap_md: - Both the DFT and the IDFT produce results that are periodic in both dimensions.- The periods are defined by the dimensions $N$ and $M$ of the discrete signal.

concepts.one_liner: The decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique, meaning only one specific linear combination exists for any given signal.

concepts.motivation_md: Uniqueness ensures that the frequency representation of a signal is well-defined, allowing for consistent analysis and perfect reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Any signal has exactly one representation as a sum of complex exponential basis functions.- This uniqueness guarantees that the Fourier coefficients for a signal are distinct and unambiguous.

concepts.title: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
concepts.one_liner: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is an efficient algorithm that reduces the computational complexity of the DFT from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.content: The DFT became very popular thanks to the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. The most common FFT algorithm is the Cooley–Tukey algorithm, which reduces the computation cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Before the FFT, calculating the DFT for large signals was computationally prohibitive; the FFT's efficiency made real-time digital signal processing and modern image analysis possible.
concepts.recap_md: - The FFT is a highly efficient algorithm for computing the Discrete Fourier Transform.- It reduces computational complexity from quadratic $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.- The Cooley–Tukey algorithm is the most widely used implementation of the FFT.

concepts.title: Spatial Frequency
concepts.one_liner: Spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space, providing a precise language for analyzing image components like sharpness and blur.
concepts.content: Spatial frequency provides a precise language to describe image components and the effects of linear filters, moving beyond informal terms like "sharp" or "blurry." By analogy with temporal frequencies that describe variation over time, a spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space. The Fourier transform allows a signal to be represented as a sum of complex exponentials, each corresponding to a different spatial frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: We need a more precise language to talk about the effect of linear filters, and the different image components, than to say "sharp" and "blurry" parts of the image.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Spatial frequency quantifies the rate of change in an image's intensity across its dimensions.", "- High spatial frequencies correspond to sharp edges and fine details, while low frequencies correspond to smooth gradients." ]

concepts.title: Image Transforms as Representation Change
concepts.one_liner: Image transforms convert pixel data into alternative representations to reveal properties useful for solving vision tasks.
concepts.content: Image transforms convert pixel data into alternative representations that can reveal properties useful for solving vision tasks. A linear image transform of the form $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ changes the initial pixel representation into an intermediate representation $\mathbf{x}$, which may not be an image. Such representations are particularly valuable when they are invertible, allowing the original pixels to be recovered via $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}= \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{x}$. The Fourier transform is a prominent example of a representation that offers properties not immediately available in the original pixel data.

concepts.title: Campbell and Robson chart
concepts.one_liner: The Campbell and Robson chart is a separable image used to experience the human visual system's transfer function through varying frequency and amplitude.
concepts.content: To experience the transfer function of our own visual system, we can build an $N \times M$ image defined by $\ell\left[n,m\right] = A\left[m\right] \sin(2 \pi f\left[n\right] n/N)$. This image is separable and is composed of two factors: an amplitude, $A\left[m\right]$, that varies only along the vertical dimension, $m$, and a wave with a frequency, $f\left[n\right]$, that varies along the horizontal component, $n$. The amplitude, $A\left[m\right] = A_{min} (A_{max}/A_{min})^{m/M}$, goes from $A_{max}$ to $A_{min}$ on a logarithmic scale. The frequency function, $f\left[n\right] = f_{min} (f_{max}/f_{min})^{n/N}$, is defined as an increasing function that starts from $f_{min}=1$ and grows up to $f_{max}=60$. This image, shown in (see figure: Contrast sensitivity function shown by the Campbell and Robson chart. The image shows a sine wave of increasing frequency from left to right, and increasing amplitude from top to bottom. Can you...), is also called the Campbell and Robson chart. It appears to an observer as a signal with a wave that oscillates slow at the left and faster toward the right and that has high contrast at the bottom and loses contrast towards the top becoming invisible.
concepts.motivation_md: This chart provides a visual demonstration of how human contrast sensitivity depends on spatial frequency, making the abstract concept of a transfer function visible to the observer.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses a sine wave with frequency increasing horizontally and amplitude decreasing vertically. - The chart reveals the limits of human perception across different spatial frequencies.

concepts.title: Contrast sensitivity function (CSF)
concepts.one_liner: The contrast sensitivity function (CSF) describes the human visual system's sensitivity to different spatial frequencies, acting like a band-pass filter.
concepts.content: The Campbell and Robson chart is not perceived as being separable. If you trace the region where the sine wave seems to disappear, you will trace a curve. In fact, your visual system acts like a band-pass filter: you are sensitive to middle spatial frequencies (peaking around 6 cycles/degree) and less sensitive to very low spatial frequencies and high spatial frequencies. concepts.title: Locality vs. globality in Fourier representation
concepts.one_liner: While the Fourier transform is powerful for frequency analysis, it lacks spatial localization because its sinusoidal components cover the entire image.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform is an indispensable tool for linear systems analysis, image analysis, and for efficient filter output computation. Among the benefits of the Fourier transform representation are that it's easy to analyze images according to spatial frequency, representing progress over a mere pixel representation. But the Fourier transform has a major drawback as an image representation: it's too global! Every sinusoidal component covers the entire image. The Fourier transform tells us a little about what is happening in the image (based on the spatial frequency content), but it tells us nothing about where it is happening. Conversely, a pixel representation gives great spatial localization, but a pixel value by itself doesn't help us learn much about what's going on in the image. We seek a representation that's somewhere in between those two extremes.

concepts.title: Fourier Series
concepts.one_liner: Joseph Fourier showed that any periodic signal can be written as an infinite sum of trigonometric functions.
concepts.content: In 1822, French mathematician and engineer Joseph Fourier, as part of his work on the study on heat propagation, showed that any periodic signal could be written as an infinite sum of trigonometric functions (cosine and sine functions). His ideas were published in his famous book *Theorie de la Chaleur*, and the Fourier series has become one of the most important mathematical tools in science and engineering.

concepts.title: Fourier's Theorem on Periodic Signals
concepts.one_liner: Any function defined on $(0, \pi)$ can be expressed as an infinite linear combination of harmonically related sinusoids.
concepts.content: Fourier showed that any function, $\ell(t)$ defined in the interval $t \in (0,\pi)$, could be expressed as an infinite linear combination of harmonically related sinusoids, $$\ell(t) = a_1 \sin (t) + a_2 \sin (2t) + a_3 \sin (3t) + ...$$ and that the value of the coefficients $a_n$ could be computed as the area of the curve $\ell(t) \sin (nt)$. Precisely, $$a_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi  \ell(t) \sin (nt) dt$$

concepts.title: Continuous Time Sine Wave
concepts.one_liner: A continuous time sine wave is defined by its amplitude, frequency, and phase.
concepts.content: The continuous time sine wave is $$s\left(t\right) = A \sin\left(w ~t - \theta \right)$$ where $A$ is the amplitude, $w$ is the frequency, and $\theta$ is the phase. The wave signal is periodic with a period $T=2 \pi / w$. [FIGURE:61cdacec6e8491fb | ]

concepts.title: Discrete Time Sine Wave
concepts.one_liner: A discrete time sine wave is periodic only if its frequency is a rational multiple of $2\pi$.
concepts.content: In discrete time, the discrete time sine wave is $s\left[n\right] = A \sin\left(w ~n - \theta \right)$. Note that the discrete sine wave will not be periodic for any arbitrary value of $w$. For the wave to be periodic, the frequency has to be $w = 2 \pi K / N$ for $K,N \in \mathbb{N}$. If $K/N$ is an irreducible fraction, then the period of the wave will be $T = N$ samples. Although $\theta$ can have any value, we consider only $\theta=0$ and $\theta = \pi/2$, which correspond to the sine and cosine waves, respectively. To make explicit the periodicity of the wave, we use the forms $s_k\left[n\right] = \sin\left( \frac{2 \pi}{N} \, k \, n \right)$ and $c_k\left[n\right] = \cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N} \,k\,n \right)$. This notation is used for periodic signals with period $N$, where $k \in \left[1, N/2\right]$ denotes the frequency. If $k=0$, then $s\left[n\right] = 0$ and $c\left[n\right]=1$. Since $c_{N-k} = c_k$ and $s_{N-k} = -s_k$, frequencies $k>N/2$ yield the same waves as those in the interval $[1, N/2]$. For example, with $A=1$ and $N=20$, if $k=3$ the wave oscillates three times in the interval $[0, N-1]$, but is only truly periodic every $N$ samples because $3/20$ is an irreducible fraction.

concepts.recap_md: - Discrete sine waves are periodic only if the frequency $w$ is a rational multiple of $2\pi$. - The period $T$ is determined by the denominator of the irreducible frequency fraction. - Frequencies $k > N/2$ produce the same set of waves as those in the interval $[1, N/2]$.

concepts.title: Periodicity of Discrete Signals
concepts.one_liner: A discrete signal is periodic if it repeats its values exactly every $T$ integer steps.

concepts.title: 2D Sine and Cosine Waves
concepts.one_liner: Two-dimensional sine and cosine waves are defined by spatial frequencies along two dimensions.
concepts.content: The analysis of sine waves can be extended to two dimensions (2D). (see figure: 2D sine waves with $N=M=20$. The frequency values are (a) $u=2, v=0$; (b) $u=3, v=1$; (c) $u=7,v=-5$.)
